title: Rescan Instead of Giving Up: Getting the Next Frame Back

questions.question: A byte goes missing from the middle of a frame and the checksum fails. What does the parser from lesson 08-02 do with the bytes it took?
options: Throws them all away, including the start of the next real frame it reached into to make up the length
Keeps them for the next attempt
Repairs the frame from the checksum
Asks the device to send it again
questions.explanation: The length was a promise the missing byte broke, so the parser reached into the next frame to keep it. Discarding the candidate discards that frame's start as well.

questions.question: On a failed checksum the rescanning parser gives up the start byte alone. Why not the whole candidate?
options: A failed checksum says the bytes do not form a frame from this start byte, and says nothing about whether one starts later inside them
The start byte is the only part that can be wrong
It is faster to discard one byte
questions.explanation: The next real frame may begin inside the bytes just read. Searching again from the next byte finds it, and the cost when it is not there is one comparison.

questions.question: Why does the parser need next() as well as push()?
options: A rescan can leave a second whole frame in the window, and without a way to look again with no new byte it waits for one, which on a quiet device is a long time
questions.explanation: A false claim can contain two real frames. The first is returned by push(); the second must be collected by next(), or it is delivered late.

questions.question: Why is the length byte checked before it is used, in a parser that holds bytes?
options: It comes off a wire, and it decides how many bytes to wait for
questions.explanation: A claim larger than the window would wait for bytes there is no room to keep. A claim is not a fact. Checked against the window and against the size of the check, it is counted as malformed and the start byte is given up.

questions.question: Rescanning delivered 44737 frames against 40747 for the old parser, and 13 wrong frames against 11. What explains the extra wrong ones?
options: It examines more candidate frames, and each is another one in 256 chance for an eight bit checksum to pass by luck
questions.explanation: Recovering frames means trying more alignments, and more alignments means more chances for a misaligned one to match. The cure is a wider check, not less scanning.

questions.question: CRC-16 let 0 wrong frames through where CRC-8 let 13. What did it cost?
options: One more byte on every frame, which is ten percent more on a ten byte frame, and it makes a wrong pass 256 times rarer rather than impossible
questions.explanation: Wider is rarer, never zero. Whether the byte is worth it depends on how many frames a second the link carries and how noisy it is.
